title-info.book-title: The Measure of a Long Afternoon

annotation.p: An English test book for unit recognition. It mixes metric and imperial units in long and abbreviated forms, including metres, feet, miles, millimetres, grams, pounds, litres, gallons, Celsius, Fahrenheit, and speed units.

title.p: The Measure of a Long Afternoon
A field notebook in two systems

section.p: The old survey station stood at the edge of the meadow, exactly 5 ft from the wooden fence. Its roof was three metres wide and nearly 700 mm above the door frame. A faded sign claimed that the building had been erected in 1924, when measurements were written in feet and inches, though the newer inspection label preferred metres and centimetres.

Before breakfast, Mara walked around the station with a steel tape. The eastern wall measured 12 metres, or just over 39 feet. The western wall was 11.98 m, which the caretaker called 39 ft 4 in because he trusted his old brass ruler more than the decimal markings.

Inside, a narrow table was 1.8 metres long and 600 mm deep. Someone had placed a 12-inch ruler beside it, as if the two systems were having a quiet argument. On the table sat a notebook, a compass, and a paper cup holding 250 ml of black coffee.

The first marker was 400 metres from the station. The second was half a mile away, or about 805 metres if the map was correct. Between them ran a path no wider than 3 ft, with wet grass brushing both sides of the boots.

At the halfway point, Mara found a metal post leaning at an angle. Its top was 2.4 m above the ground, but the post had sunk 8 inches into the soil. She measured the exposed section again: 7 feet 6 inches, then 2.29 metres, then 2290 mm. All three notes described the same post.

A wooden crate lay beside the marker. The label said its mass was 18 kg. The delivery tag, printed several years earlier, said 40 lb. It also listed a volume of 2 gallons, although the crate looked far too small to hold that much water. Mara wrote both values in the margin and continued toward the stream.

The stream was only 14 feet across at the shallow crossing, but the current was strong after two days of rain. Its surface stood 30 cm below the bank. A yellow gauge showed 700 mm, while a handwritten note beside it said 2 ft 4 in. The numbers differed by a few millimetres, probably because the gauge had shifted overnight.

Mara tested the water temperature. The digital instrument displayed 12 degrees Celsius. The old thermometer beside it read 54 degrees Fahrenheit. She recorded both temperatures, then added a small note: 12 C is cool enough for a short crossing, but not for a long swim.

The bridge downstream was 18 metres long and 1 metre wide. A warning board advised visitors not to exceed 220 lb. Mara weighed her pack at 9 kg, or approximately 20 lb, and decided that the bridge would tolerate one traveller at a time.

Beyond the stream, the path became a road. The sign at the junction said NORTH RIDGE 3 mi. A newer trail marker gave the same distance as 4.8 km. Between the two signs, a painted arrow pointed toward a village 2 miles away, or 3.2 kilometres if one followed the paved route instead of the old cart track.

The climb rose 120 metres over a distance of 1.5 km. In the notebook, Mara described the slope as “about 400 ft in one mile.” The first sentence was precise, the second was easier for the road crew to understand.

At the top, a wind gauge spun steadily. It reported 25 kilometres per hour, while the small dial beside it marked 15 mph. The air temperature had fallen to 8 C, or 46 F. Mara pulled on a jacket and measured the lookout platform: 10 m by 6 m, with a railing 1.1 metres high, approximately 3 ft 7 in.

The workshop at North Ridge was built from stone blocks, each nearly 300 mm long. The main door was 7 feet high and 4 ft wide. A newer replacement door had been ordered as 2130 mm by 1220 mm, but the carpenter had written 84 in by 48 in on the invoice.

On a shelf were containers of different sizes. One held 500 grams of nails. Another held 2 pounds of bolts. A blue can was marked 1 litre, while an older red can was marked 1 pint. The labels were not interchangeable: a litre is larger than an imperial pint, and neither one should be confused with a US pint.

The workshop stove was rated at 18,000 BTU per hour. Its pipe rose 2 metres through the roof, then extended 6 inches above the ridge. The owner said the firebox could hold 4 lb of coal or 1.8 kg, depending on which scale was nearest.

By evening, Mara had travelled 9.6 km, a little under 6 miles. She had climbed 340 metres, crossed one stream, and consumed 750 ml of water. Her food ration was 120 g of bread, 80 g of cheese, and a chocolate bar weighing 2 oz.

She made one final survey beside the workshop. A row of lamps stood 20 metres apart, or about 66 feet. The nearest lamp was 5 m from the door. The farthest lamp was 100 metres away, more than 300 ft across the dark yard.

At 9 pm, the temperature was 5 degrees Celsius, or 41 degrees Fahrenheit. The wind had dropped to 4 km/h, less than 3 mph. Mara closed the notebook and wrote the conclusion in both forms: the ridge was 480 metres high, approximately 1575 feet, and the entire route covered 10 kilometres, approximately 6.2 miles.

Tomorrow she would return to the station. The road would still be 3 miles long, the bridge would still be 18 metres, and the old sign would still disagree with the new one. That was the useful thing about measurements: even when the units changed, the hill remained exactly where it was.
